nodes.label: William Cronon
nodes.date_label: Changes in the Land 1983 · Nature’s Metropolis 1991 · “The Trouble with Wilderness” 1995 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: A historian of North American environments who treats ecological change as a two-way relation between people and the rest of nature, worked out through property, markets and ideas of nature. Changes in the Land (1983) assumes that 'the interactions of the two are dialectical' and finds in colonial New England not a choice between landscapes with and without people but 'two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'. Nature’s Metropolis (1991) follows grain, lumber and meat between Chicago and its hinterland on the premise that 'city and country have a common history, so their stories are best told together'. 'A Place for Stories' (1992) asks environmental historians for 'stories about stories about nature', and 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995) calls wilderness 'quite profoundly a human creation'. Reviewers found the Chicago book distant from farmers and townspeople, or moralising; he replied that he saw 'no pure heroes or pure villains'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: William Cronon (b. 1954); Changes in the Land: Indians, Colonists, and the Ecology of New England (1983); “Modes of Prophecy and Production: Placing Nature in History” (JAH 1990); Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991); “Kennecott Journey: The Paths out of Town” (1992); “A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative” (JAH 1992); “The Uses of Environmental History” (1993); “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995). Readings: the Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis, with his response (1992); Sessions’s reply on wilderness (1996); his own afterword to Changes in the Land (2003).
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-13: chapter 1 of Changes in the Land in an unpaginated web transcription; 'A Place for Stories' (JAH 1992; pp. 1347–1351 and 1369–1376 read) and 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993; OCR of the author’s scan, journal pagination); 'Kennecott Journey' (1992); passages of 'The Trouble with Wilderness' in the author’s reflow; and the 1992 Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis, with his response read in full. Nature’s Metropolis itself is unread: its words appear here only as forum contributors quote them with page numbers. 'Modes of Prophecy and Production', his 1990 response to Worster in the JAH round table, is paywalled and unread. He is not presented as a founder. He places environmental history among the 'new' histories 'born or reenergized in the wake of the 1960s' (1993, p. 2), names Nash, Hays, Worster, Merchant, Tarr and Pyne as practitioners (pp. 2–3), footnotes lessons to Crosby, Richard White, McEvoy and others (pp. 8–10), and echoes Leopold (n. 11). On Mahoney’s reading (1992, p. 492), Nature’s Metropolis demonstrates 'this fundamental urban historical premise' rather than inventing it. His approaches were contested in period: Danbom (1992, p. 503) finds 'environmental moralism'; Mahoney (p. 491) that urban and economic history 'seem only to serve the interests of environmental history'; Sessions (1996) that the wilderness essay underweights wild habitat. His 2003 afterword, McNeill (2003) and Canadian uses after 2000 are later readings.

nodes.label: Donald Worster
nodes.date_label: Nature's Economy 1977 · Dust Bowl 1979 · Rivers of Empire 1985 · 'Transformations of the Earth' 1990 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: A historian of the American Great Plains and arid West who set out a three-level model of environmental history. In 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) he wrote that 'there are three levels on which the new history proceeds': 'understanding nature itself', 'the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment', and 'the purely mental or intellectual', which together 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. His 1990 Journal of American History essay turned to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena', chiefly the capitalist transformation of agriculture, which Dust Bowl (1979) had called 'the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature'; Rivers of Empire (1985) described the West as 'a modern hydraulic society'. Merchant's 1990 response called the levels 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field' but found that the essay 'lacks a gender analysis'. Cronon (1992) read Dust Bowl as a story whose 'chief agent' is capitalism and whose plot 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Donald Worster (b. 1941); Nature's Economy: The Roots of Ecology (1977); Dust Bowl: The Southern Plains in the 1930s (1979); Rivers of Empire: Water, Aridity, and the Growth of the American West (1985); 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', in The Ends of the Earth (1988); 'Transformations of the Earth: Toward an Agroecological Perspective in History', Journal of American History (1990), reprinted in The Wealth of Nature (1993). Readings: Merchant's round-table response (1990); Cronon, 'A Place for Stories' (1992); Hennessey's review of Rivers of Empire (1987); McDean (1986).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents the three-level model in Worster's 1988 wording, checked in an abridged reprint and by full-text search of the 1988 edition, and the 1990 essay in his own 1993 reprint; the Journal of American History pages of 1990 were not reachable and are given only where another writer cites them (Isenberg 2013). Dust Bowl and Rivers of Empire are quoted at the pages given by Cronon (1992) and Hennessey (1987), with the wording confirmed by search of the original editions. He is not presented as the founder of the field or the sole author of the scheme: he grounds the idea in Aldo Leopold's call for 'an ecological interpretation of history', and Arthur McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. The scheme was contested at once: Merchant (1990) added gender and 'a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction', Cronon (1992) treated Dust Bowl as a declensionist narrative, and McDean (1986) criticised its generalisation across the Plains. The 1990 objections of White and Cronon in the round table are known here only through Isenberg (2013), a later reading.

nodes.label: Alfred W. Crosby
nodes.date_label: The Columbian Exchange 1972 · Virgin Soil Epidemics 1976 · Ecological Imperialism 1986 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: A historian of the biological consequences of European expansion. The Columbian Exchange (1972) followed pathogens, plants and animals between the Americas and the Old World after 1492, and 'Virgin Soil Epidemics' (1976) defined epidemics among peoples who, as Jones (2003, pp. 703–704) quotes the definition, 'have had no previous contact with the diseases that strike them' (the 1976 article itself is unread). Ecological Imperialism (1986) starts from the fact that 'European emigrants and their descendants are all over the place, which requires explanation', asks why 'the sun never sets on the empire of the dandelion', and suggests that 'the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component': crops, livestock, weeds and diseases helped Europeans make temperate 'Neo-Europes'. Later critics charge the model with ecological determinism and argue that the virgin-soil idea was flattened into a claim that Indigenous Americans had 'no immunity'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred W. Crosby (1931–2018); The Columbian Exchange: Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492 (1972); 'Virgin Soil Epidemics as a Factor in the Aboriginal Depopulation in America' (William and Mary Quarterly, 1976); Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986); 'The Past and Present of Environmental History' (American Historical Review, 1995). Readings: Miller's review (1987); Cook (1990); Cronon (1993); Subrahmanyam (1997); later, Jones (2003), McNeill (2003) and Isenberg (2013).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents Ecological Imperialism as its prologue states the argument (pp. 1–7 read, with the contents and acknowledgments, in the publisher's sample of the 2004 second edition; page numbers are that edition's). The Columbian Exchange (1972), 'Virgin Soil Epidemics' (1976) and the 1995 AHR essay are unread: the 1972 book is characterised from Cook (1990) and McNeill (2003), and the 1976 wording is quoted as Jones (2003) quotes it. His 1978 American Heritage essay on New England, read in full, states the disease argument in his own words: 'Innocent of immunity or experience, the Indians were helpless.' He is not presented as the founder of environmental history: the ASEH's own history lists him among several 'founding members' with Worster, Flader and Opie, and in 1982 among 'the already widely known historians'; he thanks William McNeill, who 'read the whole thing in first draft'. Contested readings: in period, Subrahmanyam (1997) calls the books 'oft-cited (and oft-criticized)', while Miller (1987) finds Crosby 'careful not to overestimate the significance of any single component'. Later, McNeill (2003) records that 'Some readers felt that Crosby had relocated historical agency (and responsibility for genocide and colonialism) from humans to wheat and whooping cough'; Isenberg (2013) judges that his analysis 'devolved into little more than ecological determinism'; Jones (2003) argues that the virgin-soil model 'has been misunderstood and misrepresented', that the 1976 article itself stressed malnutrition and 'the social chaos generated by European colonization', and that Crosby's other writings stressed lack of immunity. These are later readings, not evidence for the edges. The 2004 preface, in which he calls Pomeranz's Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario', is a later self-reading and is not used.

nodes.label: Carolyn Merchant
nodes.date_label: The Death of Nature 1980 · Ecological Revolutions 1989 · Radical Ecology 1992 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: A historian of science and environmental historian who argued in The Death of Nature (1980) that a science 'reconceptualizing reality as a machine rather than a living organism, sanctioned the domination of both nature and women'. In Ecological Revolutions (1989), a study of New England from 1600 to 1860, she treated major changes in human relations with nature as arising from tensions 'between a society’s mode of production and its ecology, and between its modes of production and reproduction', which in turn reshape consciousness. Answering Worster's three levels of ecology, production and cognition in 1990, she wrote that environmental history 'needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' and a gender analysis of each level. Her reading of Bacon's metaphors was disputed in the 1990s (Soble 1995; Pesic 1999, whom she answered in 2006), and a 1991 reviewer, praising her integration of gender, found 'painfully few people making history' in the New England book.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Carolyn Merchant (b. 1936); The Death of Nature: Women, Ecology, and the Scientific Revolution (1980); “The Theoretical Structure of Ecological Revolutions” (1987); Ecological Revolutions: Nature, Gender, and Science in New England (1989); “Gender and Environmental History” (JAH round table, 1990); Radical Ecology: The Search for a Livable World (1992). Readings: Cronon (1993); Steinberg's review (1991); Soble (1995); Leach and Green (1997); Pesic (1999); Merchant's own retrospectives (1998, 2006).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents Merchant's framework as her own in-period texts state it: the 1987 Environmental Review article and the 1990 JAH response (both read in full, original pagination); The Death of Nature (1980) and Ecological Revolutions (1989) through author-hosted reprinted excerpts (pages are the reprints'); and the 1992 conclusion to Radical Ecology (facsimile, original pages). She is not presented as the founder of environmental history or of ecofeminism. She builds on Kuhn and on Marx and Engels, on Meillassoux, Peterson and Bridenthal for reproduction, and on Worster's levels; in 1998 she credits Hessen, Zilsel, Leiss and Kubrin ('It was Kubrin’s idea that the key concept of early modern science was that matter was dead'). She separates her socialist ecofeminism from a radical feminism that 'runs the risk of perpetuating the very value hierarchies it seeks to overthrow' (1989). The Bacon reading is contested (Soble 1995 and Pesic 1999, abstracts only), Leach and Green (1997) place The Death of Nature among the ecofeminist histories they criticise, and Steinberg (1991) faults the New England book's narrative. McNeill (2003) and Merchant's 2006 Isis response are later readings, not evidence for the 1980–1992 framework.

nodes.label: Richard White
nodes.date_label: Land Use, Environment, and Social Change 1980 · The Roots of Dependency 1983 · field survey 1985 · The Middle Ground 1991 · The Organic Machine 1995 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: A historian of the American West, of Native American history and of environmental history. The Middle Ground (1991; quoted from Cambridge Core first-page excerpts of the introduction and chapters) rejects accounts of Indian–white contact with 'but two outcomes', conquest or persistence, because contact 'creates as well as destroys': in the Great Lakes pays d'en haut, French and Algonquian allies 'had to arrive at some common conception of suitable ways of acting', a middle ground which White describes as a process of creative and often expedient misunderstanding, sustained because whites could not simply command Indians or disregard them, until in the nineteenth century its compromises 'yielded to stark choices between assimilation and otherness'. His environmental books trace Salish and settler land use and environmental change in Island County, Washington (1980), subsistence, environment and dependency among the Choctaws, Pawnees and Navajos (1983), and the Columbia River as an organic machine, an energy system remade by human labour that keeps natural qualities, in which human work is energy as much as the river's flow (1995). His 1985 Pacific Historical Review essay surveyed environmental history as a new field, and he responded to Worster's agroecological essay in the 1990 Journal of American History round table.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Richard White (b. 1947); Land Use, Environment, and Social Change: The Shaping of Island County, Washington (1980; 1992 paperback with Cronon's foreword and a new preface); The Roots of Dependency: Subsistence, Environment, and Social Change among the Choctaws, Pawnees, and Navajos (1983); “American Environmental History: The Development of a New Historical Field” (1985); “Environmental History, Ecology, and Meaning” (1990); The Middle Ground: Indians, Empires, and Republics in the Great Lakes Region, 1650–1815 (1991); The Organic Machine: The Remaking of the Columbia River (1995); “‘Are You an Environmentalist or Do You Work for a Living?’” (1995). Readings: Savard (1992), Edmunds (1993) and D. R. Miller (1994) on The Middle Ground; Cronon's foreword (1992) to Land Use.
nodes.scope_note: Not Hayden White (node white). Witnesses for The Middle Ground: Cambridge Core first-page excerpts (full pages, folios observed) of the introduction (1991 p. ix) and of the chapters opening at pp. 50, 94 and 518; the next page of the introduction (1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi) and pp. 52–53 and 93 only in Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 twentieth-anniversary edition, whose body pagination matches 1991 at the pages checked (the equation 1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi is inferred from the introduction's opening at 1991 p. ix and 2011 p. xxv). The rest of the book is unread, and wording witnessed only by snippets is paraphrased in node text. Land Use (1980; 1992 paperback) and The Organic Machine (1995) are known from Google Books search-within snippets of their framing pages, not from page images; The Organic Machine's preface folios were not visible, so its framing is paraphrased. The Roots of Dependency (1983), the 1985 survey, the 1990 round-table response and the 1995 Uncommon Ground essay are unread (paywalled or not previewed) and are known through Cronon (1993, 1994), Worster (1990, Portuguese translation), Cook (1990), Isenberg (2013) and the publisher's records. He is not presented as a founder of environmental history: Land Use credits James Malin's neglected Great Plains studies as a trail to follow (snippet, p. 7), and Isenberg (2013) names him in a group of synthesisers. The middle ground was contested in period: Savard (1992) doubts its premise of Iroquois devastation, Edmunds (1993) finds the post-1770 chapters 'less convincing', and D. R. Miller (1994) notes the neglect of peoples neither Iroquoian nor Algonquian; Merrell's in-period critique (Into the American Woods, 1999) is known here only through White's later 2011 response. Havard (2003) and Deloria (2006) are later critiques, also known here only through that 2011 preface, a later reading. Canadian environmental historians cite him chiefly for the 1985 survey; Canadian use of The Middle Ground before 2000 is checked only in reviews and one legal article.

nodes.label: Aldo Leopold
nodes.date_label: Land ethic and ecological interpretation of history · A Sand County Almanac 1949
nodes.description: A forester, wildlife ecologist and conservationist, not a historian, whose posthumous A Sand County Almanac (1949) set out a 'land ethic' that 'changes the role of Homo sapiens from conqueror of the land-community to plain member and citizen of it'. In the same essay he wrote that an 'ecological interpretation of history' shows that 'many historical events, hitherto explained solely in terms of human enterprise, were actually biotic interactions between people and land', and took as his example the Kentucky canelands that became bluegrass under 'the cow, plow, fire, and axe of the pioneer'. He asked: 'Is history taught in this spirit? It will be, once the concept of land as a community really penetrates our intellectual life.' Environmental historians later cited the call: Worster (1988) wrote that Leopold 'projected such an alliance' between history and ecology, and Cronon (1993) described the field's subject as 'the history recorded in Aldo Leopold’s tree rings'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Aldo Leopold (1887–1948); A Sand County Almanac, and Sketches Here and There (1949), especially 'Good Oak' and 'The Land Ethic'. Readings: Nash, Wilderness and the American Mind (1967), chapter 'Aldo Leopold: Prophet'; Worster, 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) and 'Transformations of the Earth' (1990); Cronon, 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993) and History 901 syllabus (1994). Later readings: Wynn (2001); MacEachern (2002); Cronon's afterword to Changes in the Land (2003).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents Leopold as a precursor whose writing environmental historians cited, not as a historian and not as the founder of environmental history. 'The Land Ethic' and 'Good Oak' are read in two unpaginated transcriptions (the 1966 enlarged Oxford text and an excerpt of the 1949 essay); the 1949 page of the history passage (p. 205) is the one Worster (1990, n. 1) and Wynn (2001, n. 55) both cite. Worster's 1988 essay dates 'the idea of environmental history' to the 1970s, the global-predicament conferences and the environmental movement, not to Leopold. His 1990 essay, read only in Portuguese translation, cautions that the Kentucky case is more complicated than Leopold's example and needs more than a simple environmental determinism, and adds that bluegrass was a European import, which Leopold had said was not known. Cronon's 1993 uses are echoes of a moral and literary voice, not a borrowed method. Canadian writing differs: MacEachern (2002, p. 219) faults a history of Ontario conservation for assuming, without evidence, that Leopold 'was being read by Canadians, let alone influencing them' (a remark about naturalists of the 1950s, not about historians), and Wynn (2001, p. 145), a historical geographer, urges geographers to 'respond to Leopold’s call' and observes: 'Few have done so'.

nodes.label: Rachel Carson
nodes.description: A marine biologist and science writer whose Silent Spring (1962) was a catalyst for environmental concern and became a shared text for US environmental historians; it is not a work of history. The book argued that 'the central problem of our age has therefore become the contamination of man’s total environment' by persistent chemicals, followed pesticides through 'the web of life — or death — that scientists know as ecology', and called the 'control of nature' 'a phrase conceived in arrogance'. It did not reject all control: 'control must be geared to realities, not to mythical situations'. Historians who shaped the field took the book up as a starting point: John Opie's 1971 reader opens 'The Contemporary Controversy Begins' with her, and Donald Worster's history of ecological ideas (1977) places Silent Spring near the opening of 'The Age of Ecology'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Rachel Carson (1907–1964); Silent Spring (1962). Readings: Opie's reader, with Graham's account of the outcry (1971); Worster, Nature's Economy (1977); Dunlap, DDT (1981); Hays, in collaboration with Barbara D. Hays, Beauty, Health, and Permanence (1987); Nash, The Rights of Nature (1989); Cronon's graduate seminar (1994). Later readings: Lear's introduction (2002); Carruthers (2004).
nodes.scope_note: A precursor entry for a catalyst of environmental concern, not a historian. Silent Spring is quoted from the 2002 Mariner edition (a partial scan was read: pp. 1–9, 172–198, 278–279 and 296–297, with Lear's introduction); Worster's 1977 notes cite pp. 8 and 297 for the same sentences, so the pagination matches the 1962 edition at those points. She is not presented as a founder or as the catalyst of environmental history as a discipline. Worster (1977; Internet Archive full-text search, page located by the index) credits her with launching the recent ecology movement, which is the movement, not the field. The disciplinary claim is a later, geographically qualified reading: Carruthers (2004) reports that Grove conceded Silent Spring's importance to the discipline only for the United States. The Canadian self-accounts read for this batch name her as 1960s context, not as a model. The book was contested from the start. Velsicol's general counsel attributed attacks on the chemical industry to sinister influences (his letter as quoted by Graham, 1970, in Opie's reader, p. 93 from a running head). Dunlap (1981, pp. 3–4 and 7 from running heads) records that defenders of DDT condemned her as a crank, and judges that she had done no original research. Nash (1989, p. 80 from a running head) finds much traditional anthropocentrism in her ethics. These three are known only through Internet Archive full-text search of borrow-only scans (page images not seen), so they are paraphrased. Lear (2002), a later reading, writes that the cancer evidence still fuels an 'acrimonious' debate. The 1962 reviews in Science (Baldwin) and Time were not read.

edges.relationship: Ecological change as a two-way relation of people and nature, traced through property, markets and ideas of nature (1983–1995)
edges.evidence_note: Cronon’s own in-period statements. Changes in the Land (1983), ch. 1 'The View from Walden', read in full in an unpaginated web transcription (page numbers not verified): 'The replacement of Indians by predominantly European populations in New England was as much an ecological as a cultural revolution'; 'An ecological history begins by assuming a dynamic and changing relationship between environment and culture, one as apt to produce contradictions as continuities. Moreover, it assumes that the interactions of the two are dialectical'; 'The choice is not between two landscapes, one with and one without a human influence; it is between two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'; 'The pig was not merely a pig but a creature bound among other things to the fence, the dandelion, and a very special definition of property'; a 'world capitalist system' draws people 'into trade and market relations which lie well beyond the boundaries of their local ecosystems'. He sets this against species-transfer accounts 'as Alfred Crosby and William H. McNeill have done', which are 'bound to be incomplete', and against functionalist ecological anthropology, which risks 'a static and ahistorical view'. In 1992 he calls Nature’s Metropolis 'a natural sequel' to that book, which 'described a comparable set of environmental changes that occurred in New England as that region became linked to London’s markets' (Annals of Iowa forum, p. 517). 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993): the lesson 'When people buy and sell things in a market, they link together ecosystems and encourage change' is 'a central concern of my own work' (p. 8, n. 14, citing Changes in the Land, Nature’s Metropolis and 'Kennecott Journey'); 'The chief moral of my own version of environmental history is the one I tried to embed in the title of my book Changes in the Land. To live as human beings on this planet is to change the world around us' (p. 19); 'the material history of environmental change is simultaneously a spiritual history of human consciousness and a political economic history of human society' (p. 19); 'All environmental knowledge is culturally constructed and historically contingent—including our own' (p. 14), held together with the claim that 'the natural world exists quite apart from what we believe about it' (p. 15). 'Kennecott Journey' (1992, p. 33): 'The special task of environmental historians is to tell stories that carry us back and forth across the boundary between people and nature to reveal just how culturally constructed that boundary is—and how dependent upon natural systems it remains.' 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995, author’s reflow p. 1): wilderness is 'quite profoundly a human creation'. A contribution, not a founding: he makes the claim for materialist analysis that tries 'to finesse a full-blown determinism' on behalf of the field ('One important contribution of environmental history', 1993, p. 13), and places the field among the 'new' histories of the 1960s (p. 2). Contested in period: Danbom (1992) reads Nature’s Metropolis for its 'environmental moralism' (p. 503) and as 'a book about evil unleavened by good' (p. 506); Cronon answers 'I see no pure heroes or pure villains in the stories I tell' (p. 522). His 1990 JAH response to Worster is unread. The 2003 afterword (pp. 182–185: property analysis learned from anthropology, economics and legal theory; his own criticism of schematic capitalism and source asymmetry) is a later reading. edge_342 (anthropology → environment) and edge_343 (environment → culture) stay: they record anthropology as a resource and environmental history’s contribution to cultural history; this arrow is his own framework.

edges.relationship: City and hinterland as one history of markets and environmental change: Chicago and the Great West (1991)
edges.evidence_note: The Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis (51, Summer 1992, pp. 480–525; Cronon’s response pp. 515–525 read in full, the commentaries in part). Cronon: 'One of my most important agendas in Nature’s Metropolis was to try to convince environmental historians that the city is among the most important historical loci of environmental change, and that they must therefore grapple with urban history if they wish to understand their own subject. Surely such an argument can only strengthen the claims of urban history as a field' (p. 520); 'one really can’t understand the history of nineteenth-century Iowa … if one fails to see those places, at least in part, as portions of Chicago’s hinterland' (p. 515). The editor, Marvin Bergman, quotes the book’s premise: 'city and country have a common history, so their stories are best told together' (p. 481, quoting p. xiv). Rohrbough quotes its frontier as 'a story of metropolitan expansion, of the growing incursions of a market economy into ever more distant landscapes and communities' (p. 488, quoting p. 378). The urban historian Timothy Mahoney judges that the book 'makes significant theoretical and substantive contributions to both economic and urban history by placing urban and economic development in an environmental context' and has, 'perhaps inadvertently, brought urbanization as a “process” forward' (p. 491). A contribution, not a founding: Mahoney calls the city–hinterland link 'this fundamental urban historical premise', whose explanatory power 'Cronon’s study of Chicago demonstrates' (p. 492). Contested in period: Mahoney writes that in the book 'urban and economic history seem only to serve the interests of environmental history' (p. 491). Cronon concedes the 'rather distant and abstract quality of a bird’s-eye view' (p. 518) and calls studies of hinterland responses 'a valuable corrective to the metrocentric story of Nature’s Metropolis' (p. 519). 'Kennecott Journey' (1992, p. 39) states the same mechanism at another site: consumption 'came to be increasingly separated from the place of ecological production'. The book itself is unread here. cronon_urban_reception (2022) is a later reading. edge_720 is the group-level arrow between the two entries; see the proposed relabel.

edges.relationship: Narrative bounded by evidence, ecology and the community of scholars: an environmental historian’s answer to postmodern critiques of narrative (1992)
edges.evidence_note: 'A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative', JAH 78:4 (March 1992), author-hosted copy in journal pagination (pp. 1347–1351 and 1369–1376 read). Writing about narrative, 'we cannot avoid encountering the postmodernist assault on narrative, which calls into question not just the stories we tell but the deeper purpose that motivated us in the first place' (p. 1349). The argument is meant for all historians: 'I am urging historians to acknowledge storytelling as the necessary core even of longue durée histories … Environmental history is but one example of these, and most of my arguments apply just as readily to the others' (p. 1349, n. 5). 'I, like most practicing historians, am only willing to follow the postmodernists so far'; 'My goal throughout has been to acknowledge the immense power of narrative while still defending the past (and nature) as real things to which our storytelling must somehow conform lest it cease being history altogether' (p. 1372). Three bounds: 'our stories cannot contravene known facts about the past' and 'our stories must make ecological sense' (p. 1372); 'We write as members of communities' (p. 1373). 'To just that extent, nature coauthors our stories' (p. 1373). Against 'an endless postmodernist deconstruction of texts that fails to ground itself in history, in community, in politics, and finally in the moral problem of living on earth' he asserts 'the virtues of narrative' (p. 1374), and he asks environmental historians for 'not just stories about nature, but stories about stories about nature' (p. 1375). He reads with Hayden White’s Metahistory, Tropics of Discourse and The Content of the Form and with Novick (nn. 6, 7, 43), and credits Richard White with the argument about criticism (n. 46). The 1993 address restates it: historical wisdom 'usually comes in the form of parables, not policy recommendations or certainties' (p. 16). This is his own text; no in-period reading that places the essay in the postmodernism debate was read.

edges.relationship: Three levels of environmental history (nature, modes of production, ideas), with the capitalist transformation of agriculture as the middle level (1979–1990)
edges.evidence_note: Worster's own statements, in-period first. 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', The Ends of the Earth (1988), read in an abridged reprint and checked by full-text search of the 1988 edition, whose running heads place the passage between pp. 292 and 294 (Isenberg 2013 cites p. 293): 'There are three levels on which the new history proceeds, three clusters of issues it addresses'; 'The first deals with understanding nature itself, as organized and functioning in past times'; 'The second level in this history brings in the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment. Here we are concerned with tools and work, with the social relations that grow out of that work, with the various modes people have devised of producing goods from natural resources'; the third is 'the purely mental or intellectual, in which perceptions, ethics, laws, myths, and other structures of meaning become part of an individual's or group's dialogue with nature'; together they 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. 'Transformations of the Earth' (JAH 1990; English text checked in Worster's 1993 reprint in The Wealth of Nature, ch. 4; JAH page as cited by Isenberg): 'most environmental historians seem to have settled philosophically on a position that is at once materialist and idealist', yet the essay turns to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena' (p. 1091), and proposes that 'the single most important task for scholars in the history of modern agroecology is to trace what Karl Polanyi has called “the great transformation”'. Dust Bowl (1979) had argued: 'Capitalism, it is my contention, has been the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature' (p. 5, as quoted by Cronon 1992, p. 1363; wording confirmed in the 1979 edition). In-period readings: Merchant's 1990 response (read) calls his 'conceptual levels of ecology (natural history), production (technology and its socioeconomic relations), and cognition' 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field', while the essay 'lacks a gender analysis' and environmental history 'needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' (p. 1117). Cronon (1992, read) finds that in Dust Bowl 'the chief agent of the story is not “the pioneers” or “civilization” or “man”; it is capitalism', a plot that 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy' (p. 1363). McDean (1986) criticises the generalisation across the Plains (existing source, not re-read). A contribution, not a founding: Worster takes the idea from Aldo Leopold, who 'spoke of “an ecological interpretation of history”' (1988), and McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013, pp. 88–89) reports White's and Cronon's 1990 objections ('superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense'; 'potentially excessive materialism'), whose texts are unread here; McNeill (2003, p. 37) writes of environmental historians' theories that 'The most cogent was probably the one elaborated in slightly different versions by both Donald Worster and Arthur McEvoy', but that such theories 'have sparked no groundswells of enthusiasm'.

edges.relationship: Introduced organisms and pathogens as causes in colonial history: the Columbian exchange (1972) and ecological imperialism (1986)
edges.evidence_note: Crosby's own statement, Ecological Imperialism (1986), prologue (pp. 1–7 read; 2004-edition pagination). It opens: 'European emigrants and their descendants are all over the place, which requires explanation' (p. 2), and names 'what I shall call the Neo-Europes' (p. 2). Underlying the pull of these lands 'were factors perhaps best described as biogeographical' (p. 5). 'European flora and fauna, including human beings, can thrive in these regions if the competition is not too fierce'; 'Perhaps European humans have triumphed because of their superiority in arms, organization, and fanaticism, but what in heaven's name is the reason that the sun never sets on the empire of the dandelion? Perhaps the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component' (p. 7). The contents give chapters 'Weeds' (145), 'Animals' (171) and 'Ills' (195). His 1978 American Heritage essay on Plymouth (web text read in full; no print pages) makes the disease argument for New England: 'Disease was among the commodities, and in this trade the Indians would come off second best'; 'Innocent of immunity or experience, the Indians were helpless'; the Pilgrims survived 'thanks more to biology than religion'. In-period reception inside the field: Cronon's 1993 ASEH address (read) turns the two books into lessons of environmental history, 'When people migrate from one ecosystem to another, they carry with them other organisms—plants, animals, microbes—whose success or failure in the new location is often crucial in determining the success or failure of the migration' (p. 8) and 'Beware of bugs that come from afar' (p. 10), both footnoted to The Columbian Exchange and Ecological Imperialism (nn. 16, 25, p. 22). Cook's 1990 essay, read, takes The Columbian Exchange as the model for an ecological reading of Canadian contact: 'As Alfred W. Crosbie [sic], Jr., demonstrated so brilliantly nearly two decades ago ... contact was even more significantly the interaction of different ecologies or environments' (p. 13, n. 35). Miller's 1987 review (Medical History, read in full) calls the book 'a vividly written account of ecological transition' and finds Crosby 'careful not to overestimate the significance of any single component' (p. 374). The ASEH's history page (undated institutional account, read) records him commenting on the keynote at the society's first conference (Irvine, 1982) and lists him among 'founding members of our society such as Don Worster, Susan Flader, Alfred Crosby, and Opie himself'. A contribution, not a founding: no text read calls him the founder. Melville's adaptation of his question to Mexico (1994) is recorded in the existing melville_plague note, not rechecked. McNeill (2003, pp. 24, 33) and Isenberg (2013, p. 86), with their criticism of determinism, are later readings, not evidence for this edge.

edges.relationship: Ecological change at world scale: the biological expansion of Europe and the making of Neo-Europes, 900–1900 (1986)
edges.evidence_note: The scale and question of Ecological Imperialism (1986), prologue and contents (read; 2004-edition pagination). Other peoples expanded into adjacent lands, but 'Europeans, in contrast, seem to have leapfrogged around the globe' to Neo-Europes, 'lands thousands of kilometers from Europe and from each other' (p. 2); the book runs from 'The Norse and the Crusaders' and 'The Fortunate Isles' through 'Winds' to 'New Zealand' (contents, pp. xi–xii), and asks whether 'the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component' (p. 7). He thanks 'William McNeill, who read the whole thing in first draft' (acknowledgments, p. xxii); McNeill is the world-history synthesiser on the global entry. In-period uptake by connected history: Subrahmanyam (1997, p. 738, re-read) lists among early modern shifts 'travel, discovery and colonization as leading to an ecological shift of global dimensions', and his note 10 points to 'the oft-cited (and oft-criticized) works of Alfred Crosby (The Columbian Exchange, and Ecological Imperialism)', adding that Grove's Green Imperialism 'pays far greater attention to Asia than does Crosby'. A contribution, not a founding, and a resource with stated limits: Subrahmanyam's own note marks it as criticised and as giving Asia less attention than Grove. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: McNeill (2003, p. 32) calls it 'Perhaps the best-known among the thematically defined global-scale environmental histories'; Crosby's 2004 preface names Pomeranz's Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario' and says 'I am proud to have contributed to it' (pp. xvii, xx).

edges.relationship: Ecological revolutions: tensions between ecology, production and reproduction reshape consciousness of nature, with gender analysed at every level (1987–1990)
edges.evidence_note: Merchant's own statement of the framework, 'The Theoretical Structure of Ecological Revolutions', Environmental Review 11:4 (1987), read in full: 'My thesis is that ecological revolutions are major transformations in human relations with non-human nature. They arise from changes, tensions, and contradictions that develop between a society’s mode of production and its ecology, and between its modes of production and reproduction. Those dynamics in turn support the acceptance of new forms of consciousness, ideas, images, and world views' (pp. 265–266). 'The concepts most useful for this approach to environmental history are ecology, production, reproduction, and consciousness' (p. 267); 'An ecological approach to history asserts the idea of nature as a historical actor' (p. 267); production is twofold, 'reproduction is fourfold, having both biological and social articulations' (p. 270); 'Under capitalist patriarchy, reproduction is subordinate to production' (p. 271). Ecological Revolutions (1989), chapter 1 (reprint, Dolbeare 1996, p. 578): in each revolution 'The relations between men and women through which daily life was maintained and reproduced were radically changed.' In the 1990 JAH round table she writes that Worster's essay 'lacks a gender analysis' and that 'environmental history needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction, which interacts with the other three levels' (p. 1117); shifts of power are 'not only those between indigenous and invading cultures but also those between men and women' (p. 1121). In-period readings: Steinberg (Technology and Culture, 1991, read in full) calls her theorizing, 'especially its integration of gender into the analysis', 'a signal contribution', but adds 'There are painfully few people making history in this book' (p. 399); Cronon (1993) footnotes to Death of Nature and Ecological Revolutions the lesson that one cannot understand how a culture relates to an environment 'without examining the ways it engenders the natural world' (p. 9, n. 18). A contribution, not a founding: she takes Kuhn's and Marx's theories of revolution as 'starting points' and rejects 'the determinism Marx assigns to the economic base' (1987, p. 266), draws reproduction from Meillassoux, Peterson and Bridenthal (pp. 270–271), and adds to Worster's levels rather than replacing them (1990, p. 1117). McNeill (2003, pp. 38–39) is a later reading: the scheme 'has not attracted wide imitation within environmental history'.

edges.relationship: The Death of Nature: the mechanical philosophy's dead, inert nature legitimated manipulation and the domination of nature and women (1980)
edges.evidence_note: Merchant's own argument, The Death of Nature (1980), read in two author-hosted reprinted excerpts (pages are the reprints'). Introduction (Zimmerman, ed., Environmental Philosophy, 1993): 'The ancient identity of nature as a nurturing mother links women’s history with the history of the environment and ecological change'; we must reexamine 'a world view and a science that, by reconceptualizing reality as a machine rather than a living organism, sanctioned the domination of both nature and women' (p. 269); 'Two new ideas, those of mechanism and of the domination and mastery of nature, became core concepts of the modern world' (p. 270). On Bacon: he 'fashioned a new ethic sanctioning the exploitation of nature', though 'Bacon, of course, was not responsible for subsequent uses of his philosophy'; his courtroom imagery 'treats nature as a female to be tortured through mechanical inventions' (p. 272). Chapter excerpt (Zerzan and Carnes, eds., 1991, from 1980 pp. 192–193, 290–292, 294–295): 'Order and power together constituted control' (p. 36); 'The removal of animistic, organic assumptions about the cosmos constituted the death of nature—the most far-reaching effect of the Scientific Revolution', the mechanical order carrying 'a framework of values based on power, fully compatible with the directions taken by commercial capitalism' (p. 37). In-period reading: Cronon (1993, p. 3): 'Carolyn Merchant joined Worster in bringing an environmentalist perspective to the history of science, but combined it with a more feminist approach to argue in The Death of Nature that western science has harmed nature and women in parallel ways'. Contested: Merchant's 1998 retrospective reports early objections over 'how historical events were related to each other and especially to ideas' and 'the precise relationship between female metaphors that described nature and the social subjection of women' (p. 201). Soble (1995, abstract read) names Merchant among critics who claim 'misogynous sexual metaphors played an important role in the rise of modern science' and 'offers a defense of Bacon'; Pesic (1999, abstract read) holds that 'a close study of his works contradicts' the claim that Bacon advocated torturing nature. Leach and Green (1997, pp. 346, 348) place the book among ecofeminist histories in which 'femininity is linked a priori both “with nature” and “with the past”'; their main target is Shiva. A contribution, not a founding: she credits Hessen, Zilsel, Leiss and Kubrin (1998, pp. 199–200). Merchant's 2006 Isis response is a later reading.

edges.relationship: The middle ground: accommodation through mutual invention and creative misunderstanding between Algonquian villages and empires in the Great Lakes region, 1650–1815 (1991)
edges.evidence_note: White's own statement, The Middle Ground (1991). Introduction, p. ix (Cambridge Core first-page excerpt: the full page, folio observed): histories of Indian–white relations have had 'but two outcomes', stories 'of conquest and assimilation' or 'of cultural persistence'; their tellers 'miss a larger process and a larger truth. The meeting of sea and continent, like the meeting of whites and Indians, creates as well as destroys.' The next page (1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi; witnessed only by Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 edition, page images not seen, the 1991 page inferred) defines the middle ground, in paraphrase, as the space between cultures, between peoples, and between empires and the stateless world of villages, where differences were accommodated through creative and often expedient misunderstanding, and explains it by the long periods in which whites could neither command Indians nor ignore them. Chapter 2 opening (p. 50, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt, folio observed): French and Algonquians 'had to arrive at some common conception of suitable ways of acting; they had to create what I have already referred to as a middle ground. The creation of the middle ground involved a process of mutual invention by both the French and the Algonquians.' It rested on 'the need of people to find a means, other than force, to gain the cooperation or consent of foreigners' (p. 52), and was, in paraphrase, a product both of everyday life and of formal diplomacy between distinct peoples (p. 53) (both Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 edition; page numbers as the snippet results give them, taken to match 1991). Chapter 3 opening (p. 94, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt): the fur trade was 'a constantly changing compromise, a conduit, between two local models of the exchange'. Epilogue (p. 518, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt): 'The compromises intrinsic in the middle ground yielded to stark choices between assimilation and otherness.' In-period reception, each read in full. Savard (1992; Université de Montréal anthropologist) judges the book's circularity 'inattaquable' and suited to 'bien d'autres époques et régions de l'Amérique du Nord', but asks whether the Algonquians' shattered prior state and Iroquois military supremacy, 'cet autre mythe fondateur de la république américaine', were needed to explain it (p. 120). Edmunds (1993) calls the thesis 'a valuable model for the exploration of the Indian-French relationship' (p. 148) and the book possibly 'a landmark volume in the ethnohistory of the Great Lakes tribes', but finds 'his arguments for the period after 1770 are less convincing' (p. 149). D. R. Miller (1994, Canadian Journal of Native Studies, from the Saskatchewan Indian Federated College) calls it 'an extraordinary benchmark in the scholarship of European and Aboriginal relations' (p. 157), notes that White 'deemphasizes the specificity of a small number of groups in the larger Great Lakes region that are neither Iroquoian or Algonquian' (p. 158), and writes that 'The challenge for a similar study with emphasis upon the north side of the Great Lakes is obvious' (p. 170). The edge records a scholar's interpretation of Indigenous–imperial relations, which the Indigenous history entry lists as related scholarship; it does not make the work an Indigenous historical practice or a source of Indigenous authority. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: White's 2011 preface (Google Books search-within snippets only) answers Merrell's in-period critique (Into the American Woods, 1999; cited pp. xx–xxi) and the later critiques of Havard (Empire et métissages, 2003; p. xvi) and Deloria ('What Is the Middle Ground, Anyway?', 2006; cited p. xii; both unread here): the middle ground 'did not involve the achievement of a widespread mutual understanding and appreciation between Europeans and Indian peoples. People did not come together to love one another' (p. xxi), and he did not think that 'every time you find this process at work you would find the construction of a coherent space that is the equivalent of pays d'en haut' (p. xiii). McNeill (2003; text-layer PDF) reports that the concept 'struck historians of Japan and medieval Austria as useful for their own studies' (p. 37).

edges.relationship: Environmental change through land use, subsistence and labour: Island County (1980), the roots of Native dependency (1983) and the Columbia as an organic machine (1995), with an early survey of the field (1985)
edges.evidence_note: White's own statements, known for his books only through Google Books search-within snippets (page images not seen) and therefore paraphrased where the wording carries the claim. Land Use, Environment, and Social Change (1980; snippets of the 1992 paperback, whose body text is the 1980 text; p. 7 as given in the snippet results): White presents the book as departing somewhat from recent environmental history, which he describes as mostly a variant of intellectual and political history, by tracing the environmental impact of Indian and later intruding peoples and its consequences for their societies; on the same page he credits James Malin's Great Plains studies, ignored by most historians, as a trail to follow. In the preface to the 1992 edition (November 1991; snippet, folio xviii inferred from Google Books page ids that carry the printed folios xi, xvi and xvii) he judges his own use of ecology: 'I used ecological concepts like community, succession, climax, and ecosystem unproblematically even though within the discipline of ecology those ideas had already come under attack'. Cronon's foreword (October 1991; snippets, folio xi observed) places the book among White's contributions 'to environmental history, to the history of the American West, to Indian history, and to American history generally' and calls it 'a textbook case of an underappreciated classic' (p. xi). The Organic Machine (1995; snippets of the preface, whose printed folios were not visible, and of the conclusion, p. 112 taken from the Google Books page id, not seen as a printed folio), in paraphrase: White examines the Columbia as an organic machine, an energy system modified by human intervention that keeps natural, unmade qualities; human labour is energy as much as the river's flow or the calories salmon store for their journey; environmentalists, he argues, distance humans from nature by favouring the eye over the hand and contemplation over work; and the conclusion finds the nature in us in our labour and energy (p. 112). In-period third-party readings: Cronon (1993; OCR of the author-hosted page scan) footnotes Land Use and The Roots of Dependency (nn. 15, 23) for the lesson that 'the horse was not simply a European invader, but a complex cultural entity' (p. 9); D. R. Miller (1994; PDF read in full) calls him 'The social and environmental historian Richard White' (p. 157) and quotes The Middle Ground that dependency 'is an economic, political, and social relationship, but can also be an environmental relationship' (p. 169). On the 1985 survey (unread; paywalled): Worster (1990, read in the 2002–03 Portuguese translation, n. 5, p. 42) calls it the best effort to trace the field's emergence, 'pelo menos em uma parte influente do mundo', reporting White's view that frontier and western history was the formative influence; Cronon's 1994 graduate syllabus assigns it 'read for main themes' (p. 4); in Canada, Cook (1990) cites it (n. 4) for Turner and Webb as 'important, if declining, influences into the 1950s' (p. 6). A contribution, not a founding. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013) names White among historians who 'synthesized the material and cultural approaches to the environment' (p. 87) and quotes his 1990 round-table objection that Worster's scheme reduced culture to 'superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense' (pp. 88–89, citing JAH 76, pp. 1112–1113; the JAH text is unread).

edges.relationship: Environmental historians cite Leopold's call for 'an ecological interpretation of history' (1949) as a precedent for allying history with ecology, and his essays as a moral and literary voice
edges.evidence_note: Leopold's text, 'The Land Ethic', A Sand County Almanac (1949), read in two unpaginated transcriptions: 'That man is, in fact, only a member of a biotic team is shown by an ecological interpretation of history. Many historical events, hitherto explained solely in terms of human enterprise, were actually biotic interactions between people and land. The characteristics of the land determined the facts quite as potently as the characteristics of the men who lived on it.' After the Kentucky example: 'Is history taught in this spirit? It will be, once the concept of land as a community really penetrates our intellectual life.' Worster (1990, n. 1) and Wynn (2001, n. 55) cite the history passage at p. 205 of the 1949 edition; a paginated 1949 copy was not seen. In-period readings by historians. (1) Worster, 'Doing Environmental History' (1988), abridged reprint read (Merchant reader, 2012, pp. 2–9; reprint pages): 'Take away plant ecology and environmental history loses its foundation, its coherence, its first step' (p. 5); some scholars speak of 'ecological history' or 'historical ecology', meaning 'to insist on a tighter alliance with the science. Some years back the scientist and conservationist Aldo Leopold projected such an alliance when he spoke of “an ecological interpretation of history.”' (pp. 5–6). He then retells the Kentucky example and quotes Leopold's question about 'the plant succession inherent in this dark and bloody ground' (p. 6). (2) Worster, 'Transformations of the Earth', JAH 76 (1990), read only in Portuguese translation (Ambiente & Sociedade, 2002–03): the essay opens with Leopold, who 'reivindicou uma “interpretação ecológica da História”', and continues 'Levou algum tempo para os historiadores darem atenção ao conselho de Leopold, mas finalmente o campo da história ambiental começou a ganhar forma' (p. 23; gloss: it took historians some time to heed Leopold's advice, but the field of environmental history finally began to take shape). The English wording is unchecked. (3) Cronon, 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993), read in full: 'Environmental history tries to reconstruct the endless layers of change that we and the earth have traced upon each other. It is the history recorded in Aldo Leopold’s tree rings, the history recorded by the marks of his saw upon the good oak as he cut it down' (p. 19; n. 32, p. 22: 'The echo here is that of Leopold’s “Good Oak,” Sand County Almanac, 6-18'); n. 11 (p. 21): 'At this and several other points in this essay, I trust that readers will hear my echoes of Aldo Leopold's Sand County Almanac'. (4) Cronon's History 901 syllabus (Fall 1994) assigns 'Good Oak' in the session 'Reading the Landscape, Part I' (p. 4) and 'Thinking Like a Mountain' with Part IV, 'The Upshot', beside Nash's Wilderness and the American Mind (p. 6). (5) Nash's Wilderness and the American Mind (1967), checked at contents level only, gives him a chapter, 'Aldo Leopold: Prophet'. Bounded: Worster dates 'the idea of environmental history' to the 1970s and the environmental movement (1988, reprint p. 3), and in 1990 warns that the Kentucky facts need more than 'uma forma simples de determinismo ambiental' (p. 24; gloss: a simple form of environmental determinism). Later reading, not evidence for this edge: Cronon's 2003 afterword (pp. 174–175) recalls 'reading the landscape' workshops 'modeled on a famous course taught by Aldo Leopold as early as the 1930s' and calls the Almanac 'no less a meditation on the history of human interactions with the American land'.

edges.relationship: Silent Spring as a catalyst for environmental concern, read by US environmental historians as a starting point and a shared text (1962; readings 1971–1994)
edges.evidence_note: Witnesses. Opie (1971), Worster (1977), Dunlap (1981), Hays (1987) and Nash (1989) were read only through the Internet Archive's full-text search of borrow-only scans: passages were rebuilt from overlapping search snippets and the page images were not seen, so their wording is given here as attributed paraphrase. Pages marked 'running head' were observed in the snippets; pages marked 'by the index' are inferred. In-period readings first. (1) John Opie, ed., Americans and Environment: The Controversy over Ecology (D. C. Heath, Problems in American Civilization, 1971). Opie taught at Duquesne and founded ASEH in 1977 (ASEH history page). His introduction (p. x, between running heads) dates the modern controversy over human use of the earth to the publication of Silent Spring, which he misdates to 1960, and describes it as an essay on the irreversible damage pesticides had done to the balance of nature. Part II, 'The Contemporary Controversy Begins', opens with Carson, 'Biology or Oblivion?' (from p. 67), followed by Frank Graham Jr., 'The Resulting Outcry' (from p. 91) (contents). (2) Donald Worster, Nature's Economy (1977), credits her as the nature writer who did more than anyone to launch the recent ecology movement, and says that with Silent Spring she began a literature of ecological apocalypse (pp. 23–24, by the index); the chapter 'The Age of Ecology' (from p. 339) presents Silent Spring as showing that persistent pesticides threatened life less obviously than, and perhaps as gravely as, the atomic bomb (p. 340, between running heads 339 and 341). (3) Thomas R. Dunlap, DDT: Scientists, Citizens, and Public Policy (1981), introduction: DDT stayed a quiet issue until Silent Spring touched off a heated debate in 1962 by attacking both the chemicals and the experts who recommended them (pp. 3–4, running head), turning a quiet scientific discussion into a noisy public one (p. 7, running head); chapter 5 is 'Storm over Silent Spring'. (4) ASEH history page (an undated later account of a 1980 event; web text read): at the April 1980 Denver conference, Opie asked participants for lists of influential titles but told them 'to omit Lynn White, Jr., Roderick Nash, Clarence Glacken, Aldo Leopold, Rachel Carson, … authors whose works Opie assumed his interlocutors had all already read'. (5) Samuel P. Hays, in collaboration with Barbara D. Hays, Beauty, Health, and Permanence (1987), chapter 'The Toxic Environment': the pesticide problem gained wide public attention when Carson published Silent Spring on the dangers of pesticides to wildlife (pp. 174–75, running head). (6) Roderick Nash, The Rights of Nature (1989), sets Silent Spring beside Uncle Tom's Cabin as a book that exploded against traditional American assumptions and calls it a landmark of an ecological perspective (p. 78, by the index). (7) William Cronon, History 901 syllabus (Fall 1994; archived PDF read): Silent Spring is on the bookstore list of 'central texts' (p. 2) and is assigned, pp. 1–37, 103–27 and 187–98, for the 30 November session 'Toxic Politics' (p. 6). These readings show Silent Spring as a catalyst for environmental concern and a text US environmental historians shared; none of them says that it founded or catalysed environmental history as a discipline. Her framework, from Silent Spring (2002 Mariner edition, OCR text of a partial page scan with running heads; Worster's notes cite the same sentences at pp. 8 and 297, so the pagination matches 1962 at those points): 'The most alarming of all man’s assaults upon the environment is the contamination of air, earth, rivers, and sea with dangerous and even lethal materials' (p. 6); 'They should not be called “insecticides,” but “biocides”' (p. 8); 'They reflect the web of life — or death — that scientists know as ecology' (p. 189); 'The “control of nature” is a phrase conceived in arrogance, born of the Neanderthal age of biology and philosophy, when it was supposed that nature exists for the convenience of man' (p. 297). Later readings, labelled: the claim that Silent Spring advanced the discipline itself is Jane Carruthers's (2004, open PDF), a later and geographically qualified reading. She lists it among the stimuli to which 'the social sciences responded enthusiastically, history among them' (p. 380), and reports that Grove 'conceded that Carson’s Silent Spring had been critical to advancing the discipline' in the United States only (p. 383). Cronon's c. 2004–05 reading list puts it first under 'Classics and Precursors' (p. 1). An influence, not a founding. Criticism is recorded in the scope note: industry attacks in 1962, Dunlap's judgement that she had done no original research (p. 7), and Nash on her anthropocentrism (p. 80).

edges.relationship: Staples history as a disputed Canadian antecedent of environmental history: Cook's continuity claim (1990) and Forkey's rejection (1998)
edges.evidence_note: In-period texts first; they disagree. (1) Continuity: Ramsay Cook's W. L. Morton Lecture (1990; JCS 25:4, 1990–91) claims a long Canadian concern with environment: 'In a broad sense the writing of Canadian history has always been concerned with the environment' (p. 6). Against reading the older historians as nationalists only, he writes that nationalism 'was not a full-time interest for any of them. Certainly not Harold Innis for whom the fur trade, the cod fisheries and other staple products were the real stuff of history' (p. 6). He also marks a break: 'Innis, Lower and Creighton also struggled with the question of the impact of the North American environment on European women and men', but 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7), and 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus' (p. 7). (2) Rejection: Neil Forkey (CHR 79:1, 1998) rejects the line: 'Although the environment was an ingredient in the work of Harold A. Innis, Donald Creighton, and Arthur R.M. Lower, their studies do not serve as prototypes for Canadian environmental history'; 'In their approach, the environment exists only as a scaffolding on which human history unfolds, and not as an actor in the process' (p. 70). 'The staples model masks the essential role of social relationships and the dynamic between humans and nature', and 'More appropriate antecedents' are found in the historical geographer Andrew H. Clark (p. 71; n. 6 cites The Fur Trade in Canada and The Cod Fisheries). Classification: 'influence' here records a proposed antecedent that Canadian environmental historians disputed, not an established transmission of method; no in-period text read shows environmental historians taking up staples method, and neither position is presented as the Canadian field's. Later readings (2003–2024), labelled as such and not the evidence this edge rests on: Graeme Wynn (2003 review, p. 96) agrees that Forkey is right 'to puncture' claims 'that the staples approach represents an indigenous form of proto-environmental history'; Wynn (2004, p. 33) writes that the staples works 'focused on human uses of the environment', with 'little concern in this work for the reciprocity and mutuality of relations between people and nature'. Tina Loo (2014, p. 622) reclaims the work: 'it could be argued that some of the most influential work on the country's past was a kind of global environmental history, even if its practitioners did not call it that', naming Innis and Lower. Daniel Macfarlane's entry in NiCHE's 'Crash Course in Canadian Environmental History' (2024) holds that Innis's legacy 'still shapes many key debates and approaches in contemporary Canadian environmental history' and that, through works such as Cronon's Nature's Metropolis, the staples and metropolitan-hinterland theses 'are perhaps Canada's biggest contribution to international environmental history'. The edge records a proposed antecedent the field disagreed over; it does not say that Innis wrote environmental history or founded the field. Innis's books are unread here.

edge_111.relationship: Annales geography and multiple time scales as a source of ideas and a temporal affinity for environmental history, acknowledged by Worster (1990) and Cronon (1993); McNeill (2003) later reassessed the Annales treatment of environmental change while crediting their general approach as inspirational
edge_111.evidence_note: In-period acknowledgements first. Donald Worster, 'Transformations of the Earth' (JAH 1990), note 5. Witnesses: the Portuguese translation (Ambiente & Sociedade 5:2/6:1, 2002–03, p. 42, n. 5; PDF read in full) and Internet Archive full-text-search snippets of Worster's 1993 reprint in The Wealth of Nature (ch. 4, n. 5; p. 226 inferred from the running heads on either side; page images not seen; whether the reprint revised the note was not checked). The English JAH page was not reached. Because the English wording is known only from joined search snippets, it is given here as paraphrase: after reporting White's view that frontier and western history had been the formative influence on the field, Worster names French historians and geographers associated with Annales, particularly Braudel, Febvre and Le Roy Ladurie, as a further important source of ideas, distinct from the Turnerian tradition. The translation reads: 'Uma outra fonte de idéias importante, realmente retirada da influência de Frederick Jackson Turner, tem sido a dos historiadores e geógrafos franceses, particularmente Fernand Braudel, Lucien Febvre e Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie, todos associados à revista dos Annales' (p. 42, n. 5). William Cronon, 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993; OCR of the author-hosted page scan, journal pagination), p. 14: 'Perhaps this is why we feel some kinship with a Braudelian vision of history in which the different time scales of la longue durée, la vie matérielle, and l'histoire événementielle weave together to form the tapestry of the past. Although our general bias is often toward the longue durée, we understand that the interactions of environment, economy, political institutions, social norms, cultural values, and natural processes are endlessly complex' (n. 29 cites The Mediterranean). Both acknowledge a source of ideas and a kinship, not a lineage, and neither disputes it. Later reading, not evidence for the 1990–93 claim: J. R. McNeill (2003; text-layer PDF, p. 14 re-read) reassesses the Annales treatment of environmental change, writing that 'the Annales historians were, many of them, strangely blind to evolving environments'; Braudel 'normally imagined it as an unchanging force', while Le Roy Ladurie 'embraced environmental change'; 'To a very limited extent, then, Annales historians were engaged in environmental history avant la lettre'; yet 'Their general approach however proved inspirational for many who would become environmental historians'. Gurevich's chapter (publisher abstract only) supports the Annales side: geography among the school's concerns; it says nothing about environmental history. Earlier wording (an undirected comparison of affinities) is replaced because Worster and Cronon describe influence running from the Annales to the field, not a comparison between equals.

edge_720.relationship: Environmental perspectives on city–hinterland connections, assessed in period by an urban historian as a contribution to urban history (1991–92)
edge_720.evidence_note: In-period evidence: the 1992 Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis (open PDF, text layer read). The urban historian Timothy Mahoney judges that the book 'makes significant theoretical and substantive contributions to both economic and urban history by placing urban and economic development in an environmental context', and that Cronon 'has, perhaps inadvertently, brought urbanization as a “process” forward from its current relegation as a kind of assumed stage set for monographs on local occurrences in cities' (p. 491). Of the premise that 'to really understand how and why cities developed, one must study how they organized their hinterlands', he writes: 'Cronon’s study of Chicago demonstrates the explanatory power of this fundamental urban historical premise' (p. 492). He also finds that in the book 'urban and economic history seem only to serve the interests of environmental history' (p. 491). Cronon’s response: 'One of my most important agendas in Nature’s Metropolis was to try to convince environmental historians that the city is among the most important historical loci of environmental change'; 'Surely such an argument can only strengthen the claims of urban history as a field, setting the process of urbanization in a broader context that is as important to urban historians as it is to environmental ones' (p. 520). The arrow rests on one book, one urban historian’s in-period assessment and the author’s reply; it does not claim that urban history as a field adopted environmental questions. Context only, not support for the claim: Cronon’s 1993 ASEH address names Joel Tarr’s 'many studies of pollution and waste streams' (p. 3, n. 6) and cites Melosi’s Garbage in the Cities (n. 24). cronon_urban_reception (2022) is a later reading. Cronon’s own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (revision 1.131).

edge_336.relationship: Histories of the Scientific Revolution and of ideas of nature taken into environmental history
edge_336.map_label: Scientific Revolution and ideas of nature
edge_336.evidence_note: History of science supplies environmental history with accounts of how ideas of nature were made and used, here the mechanical philosophy and the domination of nature. The Berkeley retrospective and the reprinted 1980 excerpt document the case mapped; Merchant's own contribution is the separate pair of edges from her person entry (revision 1.131). Pesic’s 1999 abstract supplies a competing reading of Bacon’s metaphor, and Merchant’s 2006 response is a later reading; they document disagreement and do not settle Bacon’s intentions.

rationale: Evidence in data/extension-2026/environment-family-2026-10-13/: the field's own histories of itself (canon-evidence-international.md, 14 texts), Canadian environmental historiography (canon-evidence-canada.md, 26 texts), and Canadian History PhD citations (canada-us-canon-test/; a narrow slice, user). Cronon, Worster and Crosby are named in nearly every self-account; Merchant and White form the next tier; Leopold is the strongest non-historian precursor, and Carson a catalyst for environmental concern whose book US environmental historians shared. Thoreau is never named as a precursor. Worster (1990) and Cronon (1993) acknowledge the Annales as a source of ideas and a temporal affinity; McNeill (2003) later reassesses their treatment of environmental change. Canadian accounts disagree over Innis's staples history as an antecedent: Cook (1990) claims continuity, Forkey (1998) rejects it.

row.context: A catalyst for environmental concern rather than a historian. Silent Spring's critique of contamination and chemical control was taken up by historians of the field as a starting point and a shared text: Opie's 1971 reader opens its part 'The Contemporary Controversy Begins' with her, Worster (1977) places the book near the opening of 'The Age of Ecology', and Cronon assigned it in his 1994 graduate seminar. Contested from 1962 by chemical manufacturers; Dunlap (1981) notes that it was not original research.

Proposed as a Canadian antecedent of environmental history, and disputed in period: Cook (1990) claims continuity, counting the fur trade, the cod fisheries and other staples as 'the real stuff of history' for Innis, while noting that the older generation accepted the exploitation of the environment as 'natural and necessary'; Forkey (1998) writes that the studies of Innis, Creighton and Lower 'do not serve as prototypes'. Later reading: Loo (2014) reclaims the work as 'a kind of global environmental history'. Books unread here.
row.works: The Fur Trade in Canada (1930); The Cod Fisheries (1940)
